title: SYSK's 12 Days of Christmas… Toys: Etch A Sketch!
summary: Josh and Chuck cover the Etch A Sketch, part of a holiday toy series. They open with a list of classic toys the show has covered, then trace the toy's origins: French inventor André Cassagne (spelling settled as Cassagne in the episode's discussion, though the hosts go back and forth) reportedly got the idea from metal dust disturbed by a decal on a light switch plate at Linkrusta, a French wall-covering maker. Patent was granted to Arthur Granjean (the accountant who filed it) on July 23, 1959, with Paul Chasseigne as the partner with money. Cassagne pitched it at the 1959 Nuremberg Toy Fair, got turned down, then Ohio Art bought the license, and chief engineer Jerry Berger replaced the joystick with knobs. The toy launched in the US in 1960 with a TV commercial, and sales grew with pop culture moments such as the Romney and Obama-themed editions and the Toy Story character Etch. The hosts cover the mechanics (aluminum powder and plastic beads removed by a stylus, shaking to reset), Ohio Art's history, its 2001 near-bankruptcy and move of manufacturing to China, the sale to Spin Master, the app, the Etch A Sketch Animator, and notable artists. The episode ends with listener mail about Jerry's eating habits and miso.

segments.title: Cold open
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Etch A Sketch episode and describes how the toy works.

segments.title: Classic toys banter
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh list classic toys the show has covered before, including Slinky, Lego, Barbie, GI Joe, Hot Wheels, Easy Bake Oven, Play-Doh, Silly Putty, boomerangs, Monopoly, yo-yos, and Hula Hoops, and wonder whether Frisbees were covered.

segments.title: Toy ranking and French origins
segments.summary: Josh mentions the toy's place on a list of top toys of the century and says the Etch A Sketch has French origins.

segments.title: Linkrusta and Andre Cassagne
segments.summary: The hosts describe Linkrusta, the metal wall covering company near Paris where Andre Cassagne worked, and the wall-covering product it made.

segments.title: Origin of the idea: the decal accident
segments.summary: Cassagne was installing an electrical switch plate and peeling a decal marked with a pencil. Metal dust stuck to the decal was disturbed, leaving a line. This gave him the idea for the Etch A Sketch.

segments.title: Partner, accountant and 1959 patent
segments.summary: Cassagne lacked money and partnered with Paul Chasseigne, who owned a plastic injection molding company. Accountant Arthur Granjean filed the patent under his own name, granted July 23, 1959, then transferred it to Chasseigne; for decades people believed Granjean invented the toy.

segments.title: How the Etch A Sketch works
segments.summary: The screen is coated with aluminum powder and plastic beads, and a stylus driven by two knobs removes powder rather than adding it. Shaking resets the screen. The original design used a joystick first.

segments.title: Mechanism explained and electrostatics
segments.summary: Josh describes the pulley and gear system and an old HowStuffWorks article that took one apart. He explains the dust is held electrostatically, so the stylus removes it, and that the design has barely changed since 1962.

segments.title: Cassagne's search for a buyer
segments.summary: Cassagne asked for 100,000 dollars at the 1959 Nuremberg Toy Fair and got no takers, including Ohio Art. Ohio Art later bought the license for about 25,000 dollars.

segments.title: Ohio Art's history and metal lithography
segments.summary: Ohio Art was founded in 1908 by a dentist, Dr. Henry S. Winsler, in Archbold, Ohio. It made metal-printed picture frames and sand pails, using metal lithography.

segments.title: Chuck's metal lithography class and the license deal
segments.summary: Chuck describes metal lithography from his ninth-grade industrial arts class. Josh recounts Ohio Art's purchase of the license and a meeting with Cassagne over baguettes and champagne.

segments.title: Knobs replace the joystick and US launch
segments.summary: Chief engineer Jerry Berger replaced the joystick with knobs. The toy was rebranded Etch A Sketch and launched for the 1960 holiday season, selling about 600,000 units at 2.99 dollars.

segments.title: TV commercials and first-year success
segments.summary: The toy was one of the first to advertise on TV, with an animated rocket ship. Ohio Art manufactured through Christmas Eve to get units to the West Coast.

segments.title: Pop culture, political editions and Toy Story
segments.summary: Sales rose with pop culture moments, including red and blue Romney and Obama editions with donkey and elephant stickers. Etch appears in Toy Story. Josh notes more than 175 million sold since 1960.

segments.title: Battery versions, Animator, Doodle Sketch, and app
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Etch A Sketch Animator from the 1980s, the Doodle Sketch, the plug-and-play TV version, and a mobile app that turns photos into etch-style images, which Chuck rates half a thumb up.

segments.title: Ohio Art sells to Spin Master
segments.summary: Ohio Art sold the Etch A Sketch line to Spin Master after manufacturing moved to China around 2001, which cost about 35 jobs in Archbold. Ohio Art went back to metal lithography.

segments.title: Etch A Sketch art and artists
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Etch A Sketch art: retracing lines, using a frame line, artists George Vlasitch III, Jane Labowitch (Princess Etch A Sketch), and Ryan Burton. A locked-knob piece can be hung in a museum.

segments.title: Nate Bargatzi tangent
segments.summary: The hosts joke about shaking babies and mention comedian Nate Bargatzi.

segments.title: Listener mail on Jerry and miso
segments.summary: A listener named Kim Cooper writes about Jerry eating during episodes and the hosts respond about miso, and they give the show's new email address.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing credits for HowStuffWorks.
